title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Basophil. Under 1%; dark basophilic granules of histamine and heparin mask the bilobed nucleus; immediate hypersensitivity.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Buffy coat. Thin whitish layer of leucocytes and platelets between plasma and packed red cells.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Eosinophil. 1-4% of leucocytes; bilobed nucleus and large red-orange granules; allergy and parasites; phagocytoses immune complexes.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Lymphocyte. 20-45% of leucocytes; large round dark nucleus with a thin rim of pale blue cytoplasm; T cells and B cells of adaptive immunity.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Monocyte. The largest leucocyte (4-8%); kidney-shaped nucleus, no visible granules; becomes a macrophage in tissues.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Neutrophil. Most numerous leucocyte; nucleus with two to six lobes; fine granules; phagocytoses and kills bacteria.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Plasma. About 55% of blood: 90% water with electrolytes, nutrients, wastes and proteins (albumin for osmotic pressure, globulins for transport and immunity, fibrinogen for clotting).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Packed red cells. The heaviest layer at the bottom; its percentage of the column is the haematocrit.
Transport, regulation (temperature, pH, volume), protection against bleeding and infection.
~90% water; electrolytes, nutrients, wastes; proteins: albumin (oncotic), globulins (transport, antibodies), fibrinogen (clot).
Plasma (top), buffy coat of leucocytes and platelets (middle), red cells (bottom, haematocrit).
Biconcave, anucleate, spectrin skeleton, haemoglobin, ABO antigens, 4-6 million/µL, 120 days.
Specific: only granulocytes, type-specific contents. Azurophilic: lysosomes, all leucocytes, purple.
Neutrophil (2-6 lobes, bacteria), eosinophil (bilobed, red granules, parasites), basophil (dark granules, histamine).
Lymphocyte (T and B cells, dark round nucleus); monocyte (largest, kidney nucleus → macrophage).
Neutrophils > Lymphocytes > Monocytes > Eosinophils > Basophils.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Cement line. A layer of mineralised matrix, poor in collagen, marking the outer limit of each osteon.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Haversian (central) canal. Central channel of each osteon carrying blood vessels and nerves, lined by endosteum.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Other lamellae. Interstitial lamellae are remnants of older osteons between the new ones; outer and inner circumferential lamellae line the periosteal and endosteal surfaces.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Concentric lamellae. Rings of bone matrix around the central canal; the collagen fibres run helically, changing direction from one lamella to the next.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Osteocytes. Mature bone cells trapped in lacunae between lamellae; their processes in canaliculi link them to each other and to the central canal.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Volkmann's canals. Perforating canals running across the bone, joining Haversian canals to each other, to the periosteum and to the marrow cavity.
Reinforced concrete: type I collagen = steel bars, hydroxyapatite = cement; no mineral → flexible, no collagen → brittle.
Osteoprogenitor (stem), osteoblast (makes osteoid), osteocyte (maintains matrix), osteoclast (resorbs; from monocytes).
Large, multinucleated, Howship's lacunae, ruffled border releasing acid and enzymes.
Outer dense CT + inner osteogenic layer; Sharpey's fibres; nutrition, growth in girth, repair.
Osteons (Haversian canal, concentric lamellae, cement line), Volkmann's canals, interstitial and circumferential lamellae.
Primary (woven): first, irregular, many cells. Secondary (lamellar): mature, organised lamellae.
Intramembranous (directly from mesenchyme: flat skull bones) and endochondral (cartilage model: long bones).
Reserve, proliferative, maturation/hypertrophy, calcification, ossification.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Elastic cartilage. Like hyaline cartilage plus a dense network of elastic fibres (seen with Weigert or orcein stains); larger single chondrocytes; flexible support.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Sites of elastic cartilage. External ear (auricle), epiglottis, corniculate and cuneiform cartilages of the larynx.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Fibrocartilage. Hyaline cartilage combined with dense regular connective tissue: thick collagen bundles with chondrocytes singly or in rows; resists compression and shear.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Sites of fibrocartilage. Intervertebral disc (annulus fibrosus), menisci of the knee, pubic symphysis, some tendon insertions; it has no perichondrium.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Hyaline cartilage. The most abundant type: homogeneous, glassy, basophilic matrix whose fine type II collagen has the same refractive index as the ground substance; isogenous groups; perichondrium except on joint surfaces.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Sites of hyaline cartilage. Fetal skeleton, articular surfaces, costal cartilages, trachea and most laryngeal cartilages, external nose, epiphyseal growth plates.
Firm, resilient CT; cells + matrix; perichondrium (mostly); avascular.
Chondroblast: young, near perichondrium, secretes matrix. Chondrocyte: mature, in lacunae, isogenous groups.
Type II collagen, hyaluronan, proteoglycans (chondroitin and keratan sulphate); 95% of volume.

title: Layers and roles of the perichondrium?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: Layers and roles of the perichondrium?
body.back: Outer fibrous, inner chondrogenic; nutrition, appositional growth, repair.
Appositional: new layers at the surface from perichondrium. Interstitial: chondrocytes divide inside.
Fetal skeleton, articular surfaces, costal cartilages, trachea, larynx, nose, growth plates.
External ear, epiglottis, corniculate and cuneiform cartilages.

title: Where is fibrocartilage and what is special?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: Where is fibrocartilage and what is special?
body.back: Discs, menisci, pubic symphysis, tendon insertions; no perichondrium; collagen bundles in rows.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Connective tissue. About half of body weight; cells scattered in an extracellular matrix of fibres and ground substance; vascular except cartilage; all from mesenchyme.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Connective tissue proper. Loose (areolar) under epithelia; dense irregular with interwoven collagen (dermis, capsules); dense regular with parallel collagen (tendons, ligaments).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Connective tissue with special properties. Adipose (white and brown fat), elastic (yellow ligaments), reticular (stroma of haematopoietic and lymphoid organs) and mucous (Wharton's jelly).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Supporting connective tissue. Cartilage and bone, which bear load; blood is a connective tissue with a fluid matrix.
Cells + extracellular matrix (fibres, ground substance, tissue fluid).
Proper (loose, dense regular, dense irregular); special (adipose, elastic, reticular/haematopoietic, mucous); supporting (cartilage, bone).
Fibroblast: active, makes fibres, ground substance and degrading enzymes. Fibrocyte: resting form that can reactivate.
From bone marrow; basophilic granules of histamine and heparin; IgE receptors; allergic reactions.
α chains → hydroxylation (vit C) → glycosylation → procollagen → exocytosis → tropocollagen → fibrils → fibres.
Reticular: type III collagen networks in lymphoid organs, silver stain. Elastic: elastin + microfibrils, stretch and recoil.
Regular: parallel bundles (tendons, ligaments). Irregular: interwoven bundles (dermis, capsules).
White: one droplet, energy store. Brown: many droplets and mitochondria, heat production.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Pseudostratified columnar epithelium. One layer whose nuclei sit at different heights so it looks layered; ciliated with goblet cells in the respiratory passages.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Simple cuboidal epithelium. One layer of cube-shaped cells; kidney tubules (with microvilli in the proximal tubule) and gland ducts; absorption and secretion.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Simple columnar epithelium. One layer of tall cells, often with microvilli or goblet cells; lines the digestive tract; absorption and mucus secretion.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Simple squamous epithelium. One layer of flat cells with irregular borders; lines vessels (endothelium), lung alveoli and serous cavities (mesothelium); diffusion and filtration.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Stratified squamous epithelium. Many layers; basal cells active, surface cells flat and shed; keratinised in the epidermis, non-keratinised in the mouth, oesophagus and vagina; protection.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Transitional epithelium (urothelium). Stratified epithelium of the urinary passages: dome-shaped surface cells when empty, flattened when stretched; a barrier to urine.
From all germ layers; polarity; little matrix; close cells; junctions; basement membrane; avascular; mitotically active.
Microvilli: actin, absorption. Stereocilia: long immotile microvilli (epididymis, ear). Cilia: motile, microtubules (airways, tubes).
Tight: seal (gut barrier). Desmosome: anchor (skin). Gap: communication (heart).
Basal lamina (lucida + densa: type IV collagen, laminin, heparan sulphate) + reticular lamina (type III collagen).
Number of layers (simple, stratified, pseudostratified) + shape of surface cells (squamous, cuboidal, columnar).
Urinary passages; dome-shaped surface cells when empty, flat when stretched; impermeable barrier.
Unicellular (goblet) or multicellular; simple or compound duct; tubular, acinar or tubuloalveolar units.
Serous, mucous, seromucous; merocrine (exocytosis), apocrine (apical loss), holocrine (whole cell, sebaceous).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Muscularis externa. Inner circular layer (squeezes, forms sphincters) and outer longitudinal layer (shortens), with the myenteric plexus between them: peristalsis.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Mucosa. Lining epithelium (absorbs, secretes), lamina propria (loose CT with capillaries and most MALT) and muscularis mucosae (thin muscle for local movements).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Serosa or adventitia. Serosa = mesothelium on loose CT for intraperitoneal parts; adventitia = connective tissue blending with surroundings where there is no peritoneum.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Submucosa. Connective tissue with the larger vessels, lymphatics and nerves (submucosal plexus); elastic fibres restore shape; Brunner's glands in the duodenum.

title: Four layers of the gut wall?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: Four layers of the gut wall?
body.back: Mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa, serosa or adventitia.
Epithelium, lamina propria (loose CT, MALT), muscularis mucosae.
Submucosal (Meissner) in the submucosa; myenteric (Auerbach) between circular and longitudinal muscle.
Rugae; simple columnar mucous surface; gastric pits; glands with parietal (HCl, IF) and chief (pepsinogen) cells.

title: Four ways the small intestine increases surface?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: Four ways the small intestine increases surface?
body.back: Length, plicae circulares, villi, microvilli.

title: Cells of the crypts of Lieberkühn?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: Cells of the crypts of Lieberkühn?
body.back: Columnar, goblet, stem, Paneth and enteroendocrine (argentaffin) cells.
Duodenum: Brunner's glands in submucosa. Ileum: Peyer's patches.
No villi, many goblet cells, straight crypts, teniae coli, haustra, epiploic appendages.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Eosin. An acid dye binding basic proteins of the cytoplasm and collagen, which stain pink (acidophilic, eosinophilic).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Embedding. Tissue is dehydrated in graded ethanol, cleared, then infiltrated with paraffin or plastic resin to make a rigid block.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Fixation. Stops autolysis and preserves structure: chemical (formaldehyde; glutaraldehyde and osmium tetroxide for electron microscopy) or physical (rapid freezing).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Haematoxylin. With aluminium it acts as a positively charged basic dye binding negatively charged, basophilic structures such as nucleic acids: nuclei stain blue or purple.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Sectioning. A microtome's steel or glass blade cuts sections 1-10 µm thick, floated on water and picked up on glass slides.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Staining. Makes transparent sections visible; H&E is the routine stain, with special stains for fibres or carbohydrates.
Microscopic study of tissues and organs by sectioning, staining and examining them under a microscope.
Epithelial, connective, muscle, nervous.
Fixation, embedding (after dehydration and clearing), sectioning (1-10 µm), staining.
Chemical: formaldehyde, glutaraldehyde (+ osmium for EM). Physical: rapid freezing.
Haematoxylin (basic) binds nucleic acids: nuclei blue-purple. Eosin (acid) binds basic proteins: cytoplasm and collagen pink.
Magnification enlarges (objective × eyepiece); resolution is the ability to separate two close points.
Phase contrast (living cells), differential interference (3D look), polarising (ordered molecules), confocal, fluorescence, electron.

title: Why study sections in several planes?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: Why study sections in several planes?
body.back: A thin section is 2D; several planes or serial sections are needed to rebuild 3D structure.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: A band. Dark band equal to the length of the thick (myosin) filaments, overlapping thin filaments at its ends; its length does not change.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: H zone and M line. Central part of the A band with myosin only; the M line in its middle links the thick filaments. The H zone narrows in contraction.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: I band. Light band containing only thin (actin) filaments, bisected by the Z line; it shortens during contraction.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Sarcomere. The repeating unit from one Z line to the next; the sliding of actin over myosin shortens it and produces the cross-striations of skeletal and cardiac muscle.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Z line (disc). Anchors the thin filaments and marks each end of a sarcomere.
Skeletal: striated, multinucleated peripheral nuclei, voluntary. Cardiac: striated, branched, central nucleus, intercalated discs. Smooth: no striations, fusiform, central nucleus.
Endomysium (fibre), perimysium (fascicle), epimysium (whole muscle).
Z line; I band (actin only); A band (myosin length); H zone (myosin only) with M line.
Sarcomere, I band and H zone; the A band stays the same.
End-to-end junction of cardiomyocytes: gap junctions (electrical) + desmosomes/fascia adherens (mechanical).
Actin and myosin are not in sarcomeres; they attach to dense bodies.
T tubule flanked by two terminal cisternae of sarcoplasmic reticulum; couples excitation to calcium release.
Skeletal: limited, satellite cells. Cardiac: almost none, scar. Smooth: good, cells divide.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Axon. A single, thinner process leaving from the axon hillock, which lacks Nissl bodies; carries impulses away to synapses.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Dendrites. Usually many, thick and branching processes that carry impulses towards the cell body; they contain Nissl substance at their bases.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Myelin sheath. Lipid-rich insulating wrap: one Schwann cell per internode in the PNS, one oligodendrocyte for up to about 50 axons in the CNS; nodes of Ranvier between segments.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Cell body (perikaryon). Contains the nucleus with a prominent nucleolus and basophilic Nissl bodies, clumps of rough ER and free ribosomes.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Nerve wrappings. Endoneurium around each axon, perineurium (with tight junctions forming a barrier) around each fascicle, epineurium around the whole nerve.
Soma (nucleus, Nissl bodies), dendrites (to soma), axon (from hillock, away from soma), synaptic terminals.
Clumps of rough ER and free ribosomes; basophilic; in soma and dendrites, absent from axon hillock and axon.
Multipolar (most, motor), bipolar (retina, olfaction, inner ear), pseudounipolar (dorsal root ganglia).
Schwann: PNS, one internode of one axon. Oligodendrocyte: CNS, up to ~50 axons.
Endoneurium (each axon), perineurium (fascicle; barrier), epineurium (whole nerve).
Astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia, ependymal cells (CNS); Schwann cells, satellite cells (PNS).
Endothelium (tight junctions) + basement membrane + astrocyte foot processes.
Grey: cell bodies, glia, unmyelinated dendrites. White: myelinated fibres, no cell bodies.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Collecting duct. Cuboidal to columnar lining: principal cells (Na⁺ and water reabsorption, K⁺ secretion, primary cilium) and intercalated cells (H⁺ and HCO₃⁻ secretion).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Distal convoluted tubule. Shorter cuboidal cells without a brush border; aldosterone-driven Na⁺ reabsorption and K⁺ secretion; where it meets the vascular pole it forms the macula densa.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Juxtaglomerular apparatus. Macula densa (senses tubular fluid), juxtaglomerular cells of the afferent arteriole (renin granules) and extraglomerular mesangial cells.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Loop of Henle. U-shaped: thin segments lined by squamous epithelium, thick segments by low cuboidal cells; the thin descending limb is permeable to water, the ascending limb is not.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Proximal convoluted tubule. Cuboidal cells with acidophilic cytoplasm (many mitochondria), lysosomes and a microvillous brush border; bulk reabsorption.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Renal corpuscle. Glomerular capillary tuft inside Bowman's capsule: parietal layer of simple squamous epithelium, visceral layer of podocytes; the site of filtration.
Filtration and excretion; fluid and blood pressure balance (renin), erythropoietin; reabsorption of molecules, ions and water.
Nephron = renal corpuscle + renal tubule. Uriniferous tubule = nephron + collecting duct.
Cortical 80-85%, short loops. Juxtamedullary 15-20%, long loops deep in the medulla.

title: Three layers of the filtration barrier?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: Three layers of the filtration barrier?
body.back: Fenestrated endothelium, GBM (type IV collagen + heparan sulphate), podocyte filtration slits.
Support, contraction (angiotensin II), matrix synthesis, clearing immune complexes, cytokines and prostaglandins.

title: PCT vs DCT on a slide?
subject: subj:histo1

body.front: PCT vs DCT on a slide?
body.back: PCT: taller acidophilic cells, brush border. DCT: shorter cells, no brush border, clearer lumen.
Macula densa (DCT), juxtaglomerular cells with renin (afferent arteriole), extraglomerular mesangial cells.
Stratified, impermeable; dome cells with plaques; 2 layers in calyces, 4-5 in ureter, more in bladder.
